text: Which of the following is a defining property of living organisms that has no exception among them?
explanation: All living organisms carry out metabolism, whereas growth and reproduction are shown by some non-living things or absent in some organisms (e.g. sterile mules).

text: The basic unit of classification is the
explanation: Species is the lowest and basic taxonomic category; all higher categories are built by grouping species.

text: The system of giving every organism a two-part scientific name was popularised by
explanation: Linnaeus introduced binomial nomenclature in Species Plantarum (1753) and Systema Naturae.

text: In the scientific name Mangifera indica, the word 'indica' denotes the
explanation: The first word is the genus and the second word is the specific epithet; together they make the species name.

text: A herbarium is a
options: garden where living plants are grown for study
place where wild animals are kept in protected surroundings
store-house of collected plant specimens that are dried, pressed and preserved on sheets
collection of preserved animals in jars
explanation: Herbarium sheets carry pressed plant specimens with labels giving name, date and place of collection.

text: Which taxonomic category comes immediately above 'order' in the hierarchy?
explanation: The ascending order is species → genus → family → order → class → phylum/division → kingdom.

text: Which of these is a correctly written scientific name according to binomial rules?
explanation: The genus begins with a capital letter and the specific epithet with a small letter; when handwritten each word is underlined separately, and in print they are italicised.

text: Which statement about growth as a criterion of life is correct?
options: Growth occurs only in living organisms and never in non-living objects
In living organisms growth is from inside, while crystals and mountains grow by accumulation of material on the surface
Growth in all living organisms continues throughout life
explanation: Non-living objects can also increase in mass by external accretion, so growth alone is not a defining property; intrinsic growth is characteristic of life.

text: Consciousness, the ability to sense the surroundings and respond to stimuli, is
options: shown by all living organisms, including prokaryotes and plants
shown only by animals with a nervous system
explanation: All organisms, from bacteria to plants and animals, sense environmental factors such as light, water and temperature; consciousness is therefore a defining property of life.

text: Which of the following is NOT a taxonomical aid?
explanation: Hydroponics is soil-less culture of plants; herbaria, keys, monographs, floras, manuals, museums, zoos and botanical gardens are taxonomic aids.

text: A taxonomic key is based on
options: only the chemical composition of organisms
contrasting characters arranged in pairs called couplets
explanation: Each couplet gives two contrasting statements (lead); choosing one leads to the next couplet until the organism is identified.

text: The famous botanical garden at Kew is located in
explanation: The Royal Botanic Gardens, Kew, are in London, England; the Indian Botanical Garden is at Howrah.

text: Members of a family such as Solanaceae (potato, tomato, brinjal) are grouped together mainly on the basis of
options: their use as food by humans
the colour of their flowers only
the habitat in which they grow
vegetative and reproductive features they share
explanation: Families are groups of related genera sharing more characters than genera of different families, especially floral characters.

text: As we move up the taxonomic hierarchy from species to kingdom, the number of common characters
explanation: Higher categories include more diverse organisms, so they share fewer characters in common.

text: Which of the following pairs of organisms belongs to the same genus but different species?
explanation: Lion (Panthera leo) and tiger (Panthera tigris) both belong to the genus Panthera.

text: The term 'systematics' refers to the study of
options: diversity of organisms and their evolutionary relationships
explanation: Systematics (from systema, systematic arrangement) covers identification, nomenclature, classification and evolutionary relationships.

text: Why is reproduction not treated as an all-inclusive defining characteristic of living organisms?
options: Reproduction is shown only by unicellular organisms
Some organisms, like mules, sterile worker bees and infertile humans, cannot reproduce yet are clearly alive
explanation: Since many living individuals cannot reproduce, reproduction cannot be used as an all-inclusive defining property of life.

text: Which statement about the taxonomic category 'species' is correct?
options: Members of different species always produce fertile hybrids
A species always contains several genera
A species is a higher category than family
A species is a group of individuals with fundamental similarities that can interbreed to produce fertile offspring
explanation: Species is the basic unit; members interbreed freely in nature and produce fertile progeny, while different species are usually reproductively isolated.

text: In the name 'Mangifera indica Linn.', the abbreviation 'Linn.' indicates
options: the name of the scientist who first described the species
the place where the plant was first found
explanation: The author citation, written after the specific epithet, shows who first described the species; here it is Linnaeus.

text: A biologist finds an organism that cannot be identified with any known species. What is the correct sequence of the steps that follow?
options: Characterisation → identification as new → classification → nomenclature (naming under the codes)
Naming first, then studying its characters
explanation: An organism must first be characterised and identified, placed in a group, and then named following ICBN or ICZN rules.

text: The five-kingdom classification was proposed by
explanation: Whittaker (1969) proposed Monera, Protista, Fungi, Plantae and Animalia.

text: Which kingdom includes all prokaryotic organisms in the five-kingdom system?
explanation: Bacteria and cyanobacteria, the prokaryotes, are placed in Monera.

text: The cell wall of fungi is made mainly of
explanation: Fungal cell walls contain chitin (a nitrogen-containing polysaccharide); plants have cellulose and bacteria peptidoglycan.

text: Viroids differ from viruses in that viroids
options: have a protein coat but no nucleic acid
lack a protein coat and consist of free RNA
explanation: Viroids, discovered by T.O. Diener, are small free RNA molecules without a capsid; they cause potato spindle tuber disease.

text: Lichens are a symbiotic association between
options: fungi and roots of higher plants
explanation: The algal partner (phycobiont) makes food; the fungal partner (mycobiont) provides shelter and absorbs water and minerals. Fungus–root association is mycorrhiza.

text: Which of the following is a chrysophyte?
explanation: Chrysophytes include diatoms and golden algae (desmids); Euglena is a euglenoid, Paramecium a ciliate and Plasmodium a sporozoan.

text: Bread mould Rhizopus belongs to the fungal class
explanation: Rhizopus and Mucor have aseptate, coenocytic hyphae and are phycomycetes.

text: Which of the following is a feature of dinoflagellates?
options: A protein-rich pellicle instead of a cell wall
Absence of flagella at all stages
Cell wall of stiff cellulose plates and two flagella, one lying in a transverse groove
Silica shells that form diatomaceous earth
explanation: Dinoflagellates have cellulose plates on the outer surface and two flagella; some (Gonyaulax) cause red tides.

text: Euglenoids are unusual because they
options: photosynthesise in light but behave as heterotrophs when deprived of light
explanation: Euglena has chlorophyll and a flexible pellicle; in darkness it feeds on smaller organisms, showing mixotrophy.

text: Which fungus is commonly called a 'sac fungus' and includes yeast and Neurospora?
explanation: Ascomycetes produce ascospores inside sac-like asci; examples include Saccharomyces, Penicillium, Aspergillus and Neurospora.

text: Fungi in which only the asexual or vegetative phase is known are placed in
explanation: Deuteromycetes are the 'imperfect fungi'; when the sexual stage is discovered, the fungus is moved to its proper class. Alternaria and Trichoderma are examples.

text: Heterocysts in cyanobacteria such as Nostoc and Anabaena are specialised for
explanation: Heterocysts are thick-walled cells lacking PS II, which keep oxygen low so that nitrogenase can fix nitrogen.

text: Which group of bacteria live in extreme habitats such as hot springs, salty areas and marshy areas and have a distinctive cell wall?
explanation: Archaebacteria (halophiles, thermoacidophiles, methanogens) have a cell wall structure different from eubacteria, helping them survive extreme conditions.

text: Mycoplasma are notable because they
options: have a cell wall of chitin
lack a cell wall and are the smallest known living cells that can survive without oxygen
explanation: Mycoplasma are wall-less prokaryotes; many are pathogenic in animals and plants.

text: Tobacco mosaic virus (TMV) contains
options: RNA as its genetic material and a protein coat
only protein and no nucleic acid
explanation: TMV, the first virus to be crystallised by Stanley, has single-stranded RNA. Most plant viruses have RNA; bacteriophages usually have double-stranded DNA.

text: Methanogens, which produce methane (biogas) from the dung of ruminants, belong to
explanation: Methanogens are archaebacteria present in the gut of cows and buffaloes and in marshy areas.

text: Prions are infectious agents that consist of
options: DNA enclosed in a lipid envelope
free RNA without a protein coat
explanation: Prions are misfolded proteins that cause diseases such as bovine spongiform encephalopathy (mad cow disease) and Creutzfeldt–Jakob disease in humans.

text: Which of the following combinations correctly matches the protist group with its example?
explanation: Plasmodium (malarial parasite) is a sporozoan. Trypanosoma is a flagellate, Paramecium a ciliate, Amoeba/Entamoeba are amoeboid.

text: In basidiomycetes such as Agaricus, which statement is correct?
options: Sexual reproduction leads to basidiospores formed exogenously on basidia; sex organs are absent
Asexual spores (conidia) are the main means of reproduction
explanation: In basidiomycetes, plasmogamy is by fusion of somatic cells; karyogamy and meiosis occur in the basidium, producing four basidiospores. Asexual spores are generally absent.

text: Which feature was NOT among the main criteria used by Whittaker for the five-kingdom classification?
options: Presence of a nucleic acid in the genetic material
explanation: Whittaker used cell structure, thallus organisation, mode of nutrition, reproduction and phylogenetic relationships. All cellular organisms have nucleic acid, so it cannot separate kingdoms.

text: Slime moulds are best described as
options: saprophytic protists whose plasmodium forms fruiting bodies with spores having true walls under unfavourable conditions
prokaryotes that lack a cell wall
explanation: Slime moulds move along decaying matter as a plasmodium; under unfavourable conditions they form fruiting bodies bearing resistant spores dispersed by air.

text: The main plant body of a moss is
explanation: In bryophytes the dominant, independent plant body is the haploid gametophyte; the sporophyte is dependent on it.

text: Bryophytes are called the 'amphibians of the plant kingdom' because they
options: can photosynthesise and also feed on insects
have both haploid and diploid plant bodies
live in soil but need water for sexual reproduction
live partly in sea and partly in fresh water
explanation: Water is needed for antherozoids to swim to the archegonium, even though bryophytes grow on land.

text: The first terrestrial plants to possess vascular tissues (xylem and phloem) are
explanation: Pteridophytes such as ferns and horsetails were the first land plants with xylem and phloem.

text: In gymnosperms the ovules are
options: naked, not enclosed in an ovary
explanation: 'Gymnosperm' means naked seed; seeds remain exposed before and after fertilisation.

text: Agar, used in culture media and jellies, is obtained from
options: red algae such as Gelidium and Gracilaria
explanation: Agar is a commercial product of red algae; brown algae provide algin and red algae also carrageen.

text: Sphagnum (peat moss) is useful because it
options: has a great water-holding capacity and is used as packing material for living material
explanation: Peat from Sphagnum is used as fuel and, because it holds water, as packing material for trans-shipment of living material.

text: The stored food in brown algae (Phaeophyceae) is
explanation: Brown algae store laminarin and mannitol; red algae store floridean starch; green algae store starch.

text: Which pigment gives red algae their characteristic colour?
explanation: Rhodophyceae owe their red colour to r-phycoerythrin, which allows them to photosynthesise at great depths.

text: Selaginella and Salvinia are examples of pteridophytes that
options: are homosporous, producing one kind of spore
are heterosporous, producing microspores and megaspores
explanation: Heterospory is a precursor to the seed habit; megaspores develop into female and microspores into male gametophytes.

text: Which of the following is a feature of the gymnosperm Pinus?
options: The ovules are enclosed in an ovary
The male and female cones are borne on the same tree
explanation: Pinus is monoecious; Cycas is dioecious. Double fertilisation is unique to angiosperms.

text: Coralloid roots of Cycas are associated with
options: root nodule bacteria of the genus Rhizobium
explanation: Cycas has specialised coralloid roots harbouring cyanobacteria; Pinus roots have fungal associations (mycorrhiza).

text: In angiosperms, the endosperm is formed by fusion of
options: one male gamete with the egg
one male gamete with two polar nuclei, giving a triploid tissue
two male gametes with the egg
explanation: Triple fusion produces the primary endosperm nucleus (3n); syngamy produces the diploid zygote. Together they constitute double fertilisation.

text: The life-cycle pattern in which the free-living sporophyte is dominant and the gametophyte is reduced and multicellular (few-celled) is
options: diplontic, seen in gymnosperms and angiosperms
haplontic, seen in Volvox and Spirogyra
explanation: Seed plants show a diplontic life cycle; most algae are haplontic; bryophytes and pteridophytes are haplo-diplontic.

text: In a moss, the first stage of the gametophyte that develops directly from a spore is
explanation: The spore germinates into a creeping, green, branched filamentous protonema, from which the leafy stage develops as lateral buds.

text: Which algae show oogamous sexual reproduction among the following?
explanation: Volvox and Fucus show oogamy (large non-motile female gamete with small motile male gamete); Spirogyra is isogamous and Ulothrix isogamous.

text: The prothallus of a fern is
options: a small, free-living, photosynthetic, haploid gametophyte
a spore-producing structure on the underside of leaves
explanation: Fern spores germinate into the prothallus, which bears antheridia and archegonia; water is needed for fertilisation.

text: Which of the following pairs of features is shared by both bryophytes and pteridophytes?
options: Archegonia as female sex organs and need of water for fertilisation
explanation: Both groups bear archegonia and need water for motile antherozoids. Only pteridophytes have vascular tissue and a dominant sporophyte; neither forms seeds.

text: If the leaf cells of a moss have 8 chromosomes, the number of chromosomes in its spore mother cell and spores will be, respectively,
explanation: Moss leaves belong to the haploid gametophyte (n = 8). Spore mother cells in the capsule are diploid (2n = 16) and produce haploid spores (n = 8) by meiosis.

text: In an angiosperm, if the cells of the nucellus have 24 chromosomes, the number of chromosomes in the endosperm will be
explanation: Nucellus is maternal sporophytic tissue (2n = 24), so n = 12. Endosperm is triploid: 3 × 12 = 36.

text: In the haplo-diplontic life cycle of a pteridophyte, which is true?
options: The dominant, independent, photosynthetic, vascular sporophyte alternates with a multicellular, free-living or saprophytic haploid prothallus
The sporophyte is dependent on the gametophyte throughout
Only the haploid stage is multicellular
explanation: Pteridophytes have both multicellular phases; the sporophyte dominates. Zygotic meiosis is characteristic of the haplontic cycle.

text: Animals in which the body cavity is lined by mesoderm are called
explanation: A true coelom is lined by mesoderm on both sides; examples are annelids, molluscs, arthropods, echinoderms, hemichordates and chordates.

text: Sponges (Porifera) show which level of organisation?
explanation: Cells of sponges are loosely aggregated and do not form true tissues.

text: Cnidoblasts (cnidocytes) are characteristic of
explanation: Cnidoblasts bearing stinging nematocysts are used for anchorage, defence and capture of prey.

text: Flame cells, which help in osmoregulation and excretion, are found in
explanation: Flatworms such as Taenia and Fasciola have flame cells.

text: Which phylum is the largest in the animal kingdom?
explanation: Over two-thirds of all named species on earth are arthropods.

text: The water vascular system is a characteristic feature of
explanation: Echinoderms such as starfish use the water vascular system for locomotion, capture of food and respiration.

text: Which of the following is a mammal that lays eggs?
explanation: The platypus is an oviparous monotreme; kangaroos are marsupials and the others are viviparous placentals.

text: Bilateral symmetry with triploblastic, acoelomate organisation is characteristic of
explanation: Flatworms are triploblastic but lack a body cavity; Aschelminthes are pseudocoelomate; Cnidaria are diploblastic and radial.

text: Metamerism (metameric segmentation) is first seen in
explanation: Annelids such as earthworm show the body divided externally and internally into segments (metameres).

text: Which of the following is correctly matched with its phylum?
explanation: Pila (apple snail) is a mollusc. Ascaris is a nematode, Pheretima an annelid and Asterias an echinoderm.

text: The radula, a file-like rasping organ for feeding, is found in
explanation: The mouth of molluscs contains the radula used to scrape food.

text: Larvae of echinoderms are bilaterally symmetrical, whereas adults are
explanation: Adult echinoderms show pentamerous radial symmetry, while their larvae are bilateral.

text: Balanoglossus is placed in Hemichordata. It has
options: a stomochord in the collar region, which is not a true notochord
explanation: Hemichordates were once considered chordates, but the stomochord is now regarded as different from a notochord, so they form a separate phylum.

text: Which feature is common to all chordates at some stage of their life?
options: Notochord, dorsal hollow nerve cord and pharyngeal gill slits
Paired limbs and a four-chambered heart
explanation: These three are fundamental chordate characters; vertebrae and jaws are present only in vertebrates/gnathostomes.

text: Cartilaginous fishes (Chondrichthyes) differ from bony fishes (Osteichthyes) in having
options: gill slits not covered by an operculum and no air bladder
an operculum and an air bladder
explanation: Sharks and rays have separate uncovered gill slits and no air bladder, so they must swim continuously to avoid sinking.

text: Which class of vertebrates has a three-chambered heart (two atria, one ventricle), moist skin without scales and is poikilothermous?
explanation: Amphibians such as frogs and toads have a 3-chambered heart and moist glandular skin. Reptiles also have a usually 3-chambered heart but have dry scaly skin.

text: Pneumatic bones, which are hollow with air cavities, are characteristic of
explanation: Long bones of birds are hollow with air cavities, reducing body weight for flight.

text: Which of the following animals is correctly paired with its type of body cavity?
explanation: Roundworms have a pseudocoelom (not fully lined by mesoderm). Taenia is acoelomate, Pheretima coelomate, Hydra diploblastic without a coelom.

text: Which of the following is NOT a feature of class Mammalia?
options: Presence of a cloaca in all members
explanation: Most mammals lack a cloaca; only monotremes have one. Mammary glands, hair and usually pinnae are typical mammalian features.

text: Comb plates, used for locomotion, and bioluminescence are seen in
explanation: Ctenophores (sea walnuts, comb jellies) have eight external rows of ciliated comb plates; bioluminescence is well marked.

text: Which statement about Cyclostomata is correct?
options: They are jawless, have a sucking circular mouth and migrate to fresh water for spawning
They have bony skeletons and operculum
They have paired fins and jaws
explanation: Lampreys and hagfishes are ectoparasites on fishes; they lack jaws and scales and have 6–15 pairs of gill slits. After spawning they die, and larvae return to the sea after metamorphosis.

text: Prop roots that grow from branches and support the heavy branches are found in
explanation: Banyan has prop roots; maize and sugarcane have stilt roots; Rhizophora has pneumatophores.

text: Pneumatophores, which grow vertically upwards to obtain oxygen, are found in
explanation: Mangroves in waterlogged soil develop pneumatophores for respiration.

text: Potato is a modified
explanation: Potato has nodes ('eyes') bearing buds, showing that it is an underground stem.

text: In Opuntia, the flattened green photosynthetic structure is a modified
explanation: In Opuntia the stem is modified into a flattened phylloclade; the leaves are modified into spines.

text: Parallel venation is a characteristic of most
explanation: Monocot leaves generally show parallel venation; dicots show reticulate venation.

text: A flower in which the gynoecium occupies the highest position and other parts are below it is called
explanation: The ovary is superior in a hypogynous flower (e.g. mustard, brinjal).

text: Mango and coconut fruits are
explanation: Drupes develop from monocarpellary superior ovaries and are one-seeded with a hard stony endocarp.

text: Tendrils of pea are modified
explanation: In pea the terminal leaflets are modified into tendrils; in grapevine and cucumber tendrils are stem modifications.

text: In the racemose type of inflorescence
options: the main axis continues to grow and flowers are borne laterally in acropetal succession
the main axis terminates in a flower
flowers are borne in basipetal order
the oldest flower is at the apex
explanation: In cymose inflorescence the axis ends in a flower and flowers open in basipetal order.

text: Vexillary (papilionaceous) aestivation is characteristic of the family
explanation: Pea and bean have a large posterior standard, two lateral wings and two anterior fused keel petals.

text: Marginal placentation, in which the placenta forms a ridge along the ventral suture of the ovary, is seen in
explanation: Pea has marginal placentation; sunflower basal; Dianthus free central; china rose axile.

text: Which of the following represents epipetalous stamens?
options: Stamens fused into one bundle, as in china rose
Stamens attached to the petals, as in brinjal
Stamens fused into two bundles, as in pea
Stamens attached to the perianth, as in lily
explanation: Epiphyllous stamens attach to the perianth; monoadelphous into one bundle; diadelphous into two bundles.

text: In the floral formula, the symbol G̲ (G with a line below the number) indicates
explanation: A line below the gynoecium number shows a superior ovary; a line above shows an inferior ovary.

text: Swollen placenta with axile placentation and persistent calyx are features of the family
explanation: Solanaceae (potato family): bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary, obliquely placed carpels, swollen placenta with many ovules, berry or capsule.

text: Liliaceae flowers are characterised by
options: perianth of six tepals in two whorls (3+3) and a tricarpellary syncarpous superior ovary
five free sepals and five petals
explanation: Lily family: trimerous actinomorphic flowers, tepals 3+3, stamens 3+3, G(3) superior, axile placentation.

text: Which pair of plants shows stilt roots?
explanation: Stilt roots arise from the lower nodes of the stem in maize and sugarcane.

text: The floral formula ⊕ ⚥ K₍₅₎ C₍₅₎ A₅ G̲₍₂₎ represents a flower that is
options: zygomorphic with diadelphous stamens — typical of Fabaceae
actinomorphic, bisexual, with gamosepalous calyx, gamopetalous corolla, five free epipetalous stamens and a bicarpellary syncarpous superior ovary — typical of Solanaceae
actinomorphic with six tepals — typical of Liliaceae
explanation: Brackets indicate fusion. In the full formula the epipetalous condition is shown by an arc joining C and A; this is the brinjal/Solanum type.

text: In Fabaceae, the stamens are typically
options: six, in two whorls of three
explanation: Pea flowers have ten stamens, nine fused and one free (diadelphous), with a monocarpellary superior ovary and marginal placentation.

text: Which of the following is NOT a stem modification?
explanation: Sweet potato is a modified (tuberous) adventitious root; ginger, Colocasia and onion stems are underground stem modifications.

text: In some plants such as Australian Acacia, the petiole becomes flattened, green and leaf-like and carries out photosynthesis. This structure is a
explanation: A phyllode is a modified petiole; a phylloclade is a modified stem (Opuntia), and a cladode is a phylloclade of one internode.

text: In the monocot seed of maize, the single large shield-shaped cotyledon is called the
explanation: The scutellum lies against the endosperm; the plumule is enclosed in the coleoptile and the radicle in the coleorhiza; the aleurone layer is the protein-rich outer layer of endosperm.

text: Meristems present at the tips of roots and shoots that produce primary tissues are
explanation: Apical meristems increase the length of the plant body.

text: Intercalary meristems are found
options: at the bases of internodes and leaves, especially in grasses
explanation: Intercalary meristems help grasses regrow after grazing.

text: Which tissue provides mechanical support to growing parts of the plant such as young stems and petioles?
explanation: Collenchyma cells have pectin- and cellulose-thickened corners and are living, giving flexible support to growing organs.

text: Companion cells are associated with
explanation: Companion cells are connected to sieve tube elements by pit fields and help maintain their pressure gradient; they are absent in gymnosperms.

text: Casparian strips, made of suberin, are present in the
explanation: The Casparian strip in the radial and tangential walls of endodermal cells blocks apoplastic movement of water.

text: Vascular bundles in which xylem and phloem are on the same radius are called
explanation: Conjoint bundles occur in stems and leaves; in roots xylem and phloem alternate on different radii (radial bundles).

text: Open vascular bundles differ from closed ones in having
explanation: Dicot stem bundles are open (cambium present) and can form secondary tissues; monocot bundles are closed.

text: Which of the following is a feature of a monocot stem?
options: Vascular bundles arranged in a ring
Scattered vascular bundles, each surrounded by a sclerenchymatous bundle sheath
Presence of a distinct pith and endodermis
explanation: Monocot stems have numerous scattered, conjoint, collateral, closed bundles with a sclerenchymatous sheath, and water-containing cavities.

text: In the root, the protoxylem lies towards the periphery and metaxylem towards the centre. This arrangement is called
explanation: Roots are exarch; stems are endarch (protoxylem towards the centre).

text: Bulliform cells are found in
options: the lower epidermis of dicot leaves
the upper epidermis of grass leaves and help in rolling of leaves during water stress
explanation: When bulliform cells lose turgor, the leaves roll inward to reduce water loss.

text: Dicot leaves are dorsiventral because
options: the mesophyll is differentiated into palisade and spongy parenchyma
stomata are equal on both surfaces
explanation: In dicot leaves the upper (adaxial) side has palisade cells and the lower has spongy cells; monocot (isobilateral) leaves lack this differentiation.

text: The number of xylem bundles in a typical dicot root is
explanation: Dicot roots are usually diarch to tetrarch; monocot roots usually have more than six bundles (polyarch).

text: The cork cambium (phellogen) produces
options: secondary xylem on the inside and secondary phloem on the outside
cork (phellem) on the outside and secondary cortex (phelloderm) on the inside
explanation: Phellogen, phellem and phelloderm together form the periderm.

text: Lenticels are
options: lens-shaped openings in the periderm that allow gas exchange
explanation: Lenticels form by loosely arranged complementary cells produced by the phellogen; they occur in most woody trees.

text: Heartwood is darker and more durable than sapwood because
options: it is made of living cells that conduct water
its cells are filled with tannins, resins, oils, gums and aromatic substances and it does not conduct water
it is formed by cork cambium
explanation: Heartwood is the central, non-conducting, dead secondary xylem; sapwood is peripheral, lighter and conducts water.

text: Which statement about annual rings is correct?
options: Spring wood has narrow vessels and higher density
Annual rings are formed by cork cambium
Annual rings are typical of monocot stems
Each ring consists of spring wood (light, wide vessels) and autumn wood (dark, narrow vessels), and counting rings estimates a tree's age
explanation: Cambial activity varies with season in temperate regions; spring (early) wood is lighter and autumn (late) wood denser.

text: In a dicot stem, the interfascicular cambium arises from
options: medullary ray cells adjoining the intrafascicular cambium, by dedifferentiation
explanation: Medullary ray cells become meristematic and join with the intrafascicular cambium to form a complete cambial ring.

text: The term 'bark' refers to
options: all tissues exterior to the vascular cambium, including secondary phloem and periderm
explanation: Bark is a non-technical term for all tissues outside the vascular cambium; bark formed early in the season is soft (early) bark and that formed late in the season is hard (late) bark.

text: Which of the following features would identify a transverse section as that of a monocot root?
options: Conjoint, open vascular bundles in a ring
Scattered vascular bundles with bundle sheath
Polyarch xylem with a large, well-developed pith
explanation: Monocot roots have more than six xylem bundles and a large pith; dicot roots have 2–4 bundles and little or no pith.

text: Which of the following is NOT a component of the xylem?
explanation: Xylem consists of tracheids, vessels, xylem fibres and xylem parenchyma; companion cells belong to the phloem.

text: Epithelium made of a single layer of flat cells with irregular boundaries, found in the walls of blood vessels and air sacs of lungs, is
explanation: Simple squamous epithelium forms a diffusion boundary in alveoli and blood vessel walls.

text: Which type of muscle is striated, involuntary and shows branching?
explanation: Cardiac muscle fibres are striated, branched and connected by intercalated discs; they contract involuntarily.

text: The fluid connective tissue of the body is
explanation: Blood is a fluid connective tissue with plasma, RBCs, WBCs and platelets.

text: Tendons connect
explanation: Tendons are dense regular connective tissue; ligaments connect bone to bone.

text: The number of Malpighian tubules in a cockroach is about
explanation: About 100–150 yellowish Malpighian tubules are present at the junction of the midgut and hindgut.

text: The cockroach belongs to phylum
explanation: Periplaneta americana is an insect, class Insecta, phylum Arthropoda.

text: The heart of a cockroach consists of
options: an elongated tube with muscular walls lying along the mid-dorsal line, differentiated into 13 funnel-shaped chambers
four chambers like the human heart
explanation: The cockroach heart is tubular, with ostia on each side of the chambers; circulation is open.

text: Respiration in cockroach occurs through
options: a network of tracheae opening by 10 pairs of spiracles
explanation: Spiracles are on the lateral side of the body; tracheae branch into tracheoles that carry oxygen directly to tissues.

text: Which epithelium lines the inner surface of the fallopian tubes and bronchioles and helps move particles in a specific direction?
explanation: Cilia on the free surface beat to move mucus or the ovum in a given direction.

text: Junctions that help stop substances from leaking across a tissue are
explanation: Tight junctions seal neighbouring cells; adhering junctions cement cells; gap junctions allow ions and small molecules to pass between cells.

text: Adipose tissue is a type of
options: loose connective tissue specialised to store fat
explanation: Adipose tissue lies beneath the skin; excess nutrients are converted into fats and stored here.

text: In bone, the hard matrix is rich in
options: calcium salts and collagen fibres, with osteocytes present in lacunae
explanation: Calcium salts give bone its hardness; cartilage has chondrocytes in a pliable matrix of chondroitin salts.

text: Neuroglia, which make up more than half the volume of neural tissue in vertebrates,
explanation: Neurons are excitable cells; neuroglial cells support and protect them.

text: The mouthparts of cockroach are of the
explanation: Mouthparts include labrum, a pair of mandibles, a pair of maxillae, labium and hypopharynx.

text: In the cockroach, the crop is used for
explanation: The crop stores food; the gizzard (proventriculus) with chitinous teeth grinds food.

text: The anal cerci of a cockroach are present in
options: both sexes, while anal styles are present only in males
explanation: Anal cerci are on the 10th segment in both sexes; short anal styles arise from the 9th sternum in males.

text: The female cockroach forms an ootheca. Which statement about it is correct?
options: It is a dark reddish to blackish brown egg capsule; a female produces on average 9–10 oothecae, each containing about 14–16 eggs
Development is direct with no nymphal stage
Each ootheca contains a single egg
It is formed by the male
explanation: A female produces on average 9–10 oothecae, each containing 14–16 eggs; development is paurometabolous through nymphal stages.

text: The nervous system of a cockroach consists of
options: a single brain with no ganglia in the body
a series of fused, segmentally arranged ganglia joined by paired longitudinal connectives on the ventral side
explanation: Three ganglia lie in the thorax and six in the abdomen; the supra-oesophageal ganglion acts as the brain. The nervous system is spread throughout the body.

text: Which is the correct sequence of the alimentary canal of a cockroach?
options: Mouth → pharynx → oesophagus → crop → gizzard → midgut → hindgut (ileum, colon, rectum) → anus
Mouth → oesophagus → midgut → crop → gizzard → anus
Mouth → crop → pharynx → gizzard → oesophagus → anus
Mouth → gizzard → crop → hindgut → midgut → anus
explanation: The foregut includes pharynx, oesophagus, crop and gizzard; hepatic caecae lie at the junction of foregut and midgut.

text: Which statement about the compound eyes of cockroach is correct?
options: Each eye has a single lens like the human eye
They provide high-resolution colour vision only at night
Each eye has about 2000 hexagonal ommatidia and gives mosaic vision with more sensitivity but less resolution
They are located on the abdomen
explanation: Several ommatidia receive several images of an object, forming mosaic vision; sensitivity is high but resolution low, which is common during the night.

text: The cell theory was formulated by
options: Schleiden and Schwann, and modified by Rudolf Virchow
explanation: Schleiden (plants) and Schwann (animals) proposed that all organisms are composed of cells; Virchow added 'omnis cellula-e cellula' (cells arise from pre-existing cells).

text: Ribosomes of prokaryotic cells are of the type
explanation: Prokaryotes have 70S ribosomes (50S + 30S); eukaryotic cytoplasmic ribosomes are 80S (60S + 40S).

text: The 'powerhouse of the cell', site of aerobic respiration, is the
explanation: Mitochondria produce cellular energy in the form of ATP.

text: Which organelle is absent in animal cells but present in plant cells?
explanation: Plastids (chloroplasts, chromoplasts, leucoplasts) are found in plant cells and euglenoids; centrioles are usually absent in plant cells.

text: The fluid mosaic model of the plasma membrane was proposed by
explanation: Singer and Nicolson (1972) proposed that the quasi-fluid lipid bilayer allows lateral movement of proteins.

text: Lysosomes are rich in
options: hydrolytic enzymes active at acidic pH
explanation: Lysosomes contain lipases, proteases, carbohydrases and nucleases that are optimally active at acidic pH.

text: Which structure is the site of ribosomal RNA synthesis?
explanation: The nucleolus is a non-membrane-bound structure in the nucleus where active rRNA synthesis takes place.

text: Which of the following is NOT a part of the endomembrane system?
explanation: The endomembrane system includes ER, Golgi complex, lysosomes and vacuoles, whose functions are coordinated; mitochondria, chloroplasts and peroxisomes are not included.

text: The rough endoplasmic reticulum is mainly involved in
explanation: RER bears ribosomes on its surface; SER is the major site of lipid synthesis and steroidal hormones in animal cells.

text: Glycosylation of proteins and formation of glycolipids occur mainly in the
explanation: The Golgi apparatus is the important site of formation of glycoproteins and glycolipids, and packages materials for delivery.

text: Mesosomes in bacteria are
options: infoldings of the plasma membrane that help in cell wall formation, DNA replication and respiration
explanation: Mesosomes are extensions of the plasma membrane in the form of vesicles, tubules and lamellae.

text: The 9 + 2 arrangement of microtubules is found in
options: the axoneme of cilia and flagella of eukaryotes
explanation: Cilia and flagella have nine doublets of peripheral microtubules and a pair of central microtubules; centrioles and basal bodies show a 9 + 0 cartwheel of triplets.

text: The tonoplast is the membrane that bounds the
explanation: The tonoplast helps transport ions against the concentration gradient into the vacuole, so the concentration inside is higher than in the cytoplasm.

text: Which of the following statements about mitochondria is correct?
options: They are found only in plant cells
They have their own circular DNA, 70S ribosomes and divide by fission
They lack enzymes of the Krebs cycle
explanation: Mitochondria are double-membraned, semi-autonomous organelles; the matrix contains circular DNA, RNA molecules and 70S ribosomes.

text: Chromosomes with the centromere close to one end, forming one extremely short and one very long arm, are called
explanation: Metacentric: centromere in the middle; sub-metacentric: slightly away from middle; acrocentric: close to end; telocentric: terminal.

text: The cell wall of plants is made mainly of cellulose, hemicellulose, pectins and proteins; the middle lamella that holds neighbouring cells together is mainly composed of
explanation: The middle lamella is a layer of calcium pectate that glues adjacent cells.

text: The thylakoids of chloroplasts are arranged in stacks called
explanation: Stacks of thylakoids are grana; stroma lamellae connect grana; cristae are infoldings of the inner mitochondrial membrane.

text: Which of the following is common to both prokaryotic and eukaryotic cells?
options: Plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and genetic material
explanation: Prokaryotes lack membrane-bound organelles, but every cell has a plasma membrane, cytoplasm, ribosomes and DNA.

text: In a Gram-positive bacterium, which statement is correct?
options: Its cell wall is made of cellulose
It has an outer membrane rich in lipopolysaccharides and stains red
It retains the crystal violet (Gram) stain because of a thick peptidoglycan layer
explanation: Gram-positive bacteria take up and retain the Gram stain; Gram-negative bacteria do not retain it and have an outer lipopolysaccharide membrane.

text: The ratio of protein to lipid in the plasma membrane of human erythrocytes is approximately
options: equal amounts of protein, lipid and DNA
explanation: Biochemical studies of the human RBC membrane show approximately 52% protein and 40% lipids.

text: Satellite (SAT) chromosomes are identified by
options: a secondary constriction at a constant location that gives the appearance of a small fragment
explanation: A few chromosomes show non-staining secondary constrictions at a constant location, giving a small fragment called the satellite.

text: Which of the following is a polymer of glucose that is the main storage polysaccharide in animals?
explanation: Glycogen is stored in liver and muscles; starch is the plant storage polysaccharide and inulin is a fructose polymer.

text: The monomers of proteins are
explanation: Proteins are heteropolymers of amino acids linked by peptide bonds.

text: The bond between two monosaccharides in a disaccharide is a
explanation: Glycosidic bonds link sugar units, formed by dehydration between hydroxyl groups.

text: Which nitrogen base is found in RNA but not in DNA?
explanation: RNA has uracil in place of thymine.

text: Most enzymes are chemically
explanation: Nearly all enzymes are proteins; some nucleic acids (ribozymes) also act as catalysts.

text: Enzymes speed up reactions by
options: increasing the temperature of the cell
explanation: Enzymes provide an alternative pathway with lower activation energy, without changing the equilibrium.

text: Which of the following is a secondary metabolite?
explanation: Secondary metabolites like alkaloids, terpenoids, essential oils, toxins, lectins and pigments have no obvious role in routine physiological processes of the producer.

text: The secondary structure of a protein, such as an α-helix, is stabilised mainly by
options: hydrogen bonds between the backbone C=O and N–H groups
ionic bonds between side chains only
explanation: Primary structure is the amino acid sequence held by peptide bonds; secondary structure involves hydrogen-bonded helices and sheets.

text: Haemoglobin, consisting of four subunits (two α and two β), is an example of
explanation: Quaternary structure refers to the arrangement of more than one polypeptide chain.

text: Lecithin is an example of a
explanation: Lecithin has a phosphorylated organic compound attached to glycerol and fatty acids; phospholipids form cell membranes.

text: A nucleoside differs from a nucleotide in lacking
explanation: Nucleoside = base + sugar (e.g. adenosine); nucleotide = base + sugar + phosphate (e.g. adenylic acid).

text: Enzymes that catalyse the joining of two compounds with the breaking of a pyrophosphate or similar bond of ATP belong to the class
explanation: Ligases join C–O, C–S, C–N, P–O bonds using ATP. Lyases remove groups to form double bonds; hydrolases hydrolyse; isomerases interconvert isomers.

text: Malonate inhibits succinic dehydrogenase because it
options: is a cofactor of the enzyme
closely resembles succinate in structure and competes for the active site
binds to a site other than the active site
explanation: This is classic competitive inhibition; it can be overcome by increasing substrate concentration.

text: The protein part of an enzyme that requires a cofactor is called the
explanation: Apoenzyme + cofactor = holoenzyme; the apoenzyme alone is catalytically inactive.

text: Haem in peroxidase and catalase is an example of a
options: prosthetic group, tightly bound to the apoenzyme
explanation: Prosthetic groups are tightly bound organic cofactors; coenzymes (e.g. NAD, NADP) bind only transiently.

text: At low temperatures enzyme activity decreases because
options: the enzyme is temporarily inactivated, while at high temperature it is denatured by heat
explanation: Enzymes are inactive at low temperature but regain activity when warmed; high temperature destroys their 3-D structure.

text: The Michaelis constant (Km) of an enzyme is defined as
options: the substrate concentration at which the reaction velocity is half of the maximum velocity (Vmax)
the concentration of enzyme at Vmax
the temperature at which the enzyme denatures
the maximum velocity of the reaction
explanation: A low Km indicates high affinity of the enzyme for its substrate.

text: Which of the following statements about the Watson–Crick model of DNA is correct?
options: The two strands are antiparallel; A pairs with T by two hydrogen bonds and G pairs with C by three
The two strands run in the same direction
Each turn of the helix contains 5 base pairs
A pairs with C by two hydrogen bonds
explanation: B-DNA has about 10 base pairs per turn with a pitch of 3.4 nm; the strands are antiparallel and complementary.

text: When dried tissue is fully burnt, the ash obtained contains
options: inorganic elements and compounds such as calcium, magnesium, sulphates and phosphates
explanation: Burning oxidises all organic carbon compounds to gases; the acid-insoluble fraction (ash) contains only inorganic elements.

text: In non-competitive inhibition of an enzyme
options: the inhibitor binds at a site other than the active site, reducing Vmax, and adding more substrate does not reverse it
Vmax remains unchanged and Km increases
the inhibitor competes with the substrate for the active site
explanation: Non-competitive inhibitors change the enzyme's shape so it cannot catalyse efficiently regardless of substrate concentration.

text: Which statement about cellulose is correct?
options: It is an unbranched polymer of β-glucose that does not give a blue colour with iodine because it lacks helical structure
It is a branched polymer of α-glucose
It gives blue-black colour with iodine
It is the storage carbohydrate of animals
explanation: Starch forms helices that hold I₂ and turn blue; cellulose cannot hold iodine. Cotton fibre is cellulose.

text: DNA replication takes place during the
explanation: The amount of DNA per cell doubles in the S (synthesis) phase, but the chromosome number stays the same.

text: In a typical human cell in culture, the cell cycle lasts about
explanation: Human cells divide about once in 24 hours; yeast completes the cycle in about 90 minutes.

text: The stage of mitosis at which chromosomes align at the equatorial plate is
explanation: Metaphase chromosomes are best studied for morphology since they are maximally condensed and aligned.

text: Cells that do not divide further exit G₁ to enter an inactive stage called
explanation: Cells in G₀ remain metabolically active but no longer proliferate unless called upon.

text: Crossing over occurs during
explanation: Crossing over is the exchange of genetic material between non-sister chromatids of homologous chromosomes, mediated by recombinase.

text: Meiosis results in
explanation: Meiosis involves one round of DNA replication and two divisions, halving the chromosome number.

text: Cytokinesis in plant cells occurs by
options: formation of a cleavage furrow from the periphery
formation of a cell plate that grows from the centre towards the walls
explanation: The rigid cell wall prevents furrowing; the cell plate (middle lamella) forms from vesicles near the centre.

text: Synapsis, the pairing of homologous chromosomes, begins during
explanation: Synapsis is accompanied by formation of the synaptonemal complex; a pair of synapsed homologues is a bivalent or tetrad.

text: Chiasmata, the X-shaped points of contact between homologous chromosomes, become visible during
explanation: In diplotene the synaptonemal complex dissolves and homologues separate except at chiasmata; in oocytes of some vertebrates diplotene can last months or years.

text: Terminalisation of chiasmata takes place during
explanation: Diakinesis marks the end of prophase I: spindle forms, nucleolus disappears and the nuclear envelope breaks down.

text: In anaphase I of meiosis
options: homologous chromosomes separate while sister chromatids remain attached at their centromeres
explanation: In anaphase II the centromeres split and sister chromatids move to opposite poles.

text: The phase between the two meiotic divisions, which is short and has no DNA replication, is
explanation: Interkinesis is generally short-lived and is followed by prophase II.

text: Which of the following is a significance of mitosis?
options: It maintains the same chromosome number in daughter cells and helps in growth and repair
It produces genetic variation through crossing over
explanation: Mitosis produces genetically identical diploid cells for growth, cell repair and maintaining nucleo-cytoplasmic ratio.

text: In animal cells, during the S phase, which event occurs in the cytoplasm alongside DNA replication?
explanation: While DNA replicates in the nucleus, the centriole duplicates in the cytoplasm.

text: A cell has 40 chromosomes at G₁. The number of chromosomes and chromatids at metaphase of mitosis will be
explanation: DNA replicates in S phase, so each of the 40 chromosomes has two sister chromatids at metaphase.

text: Karyokinesis without cytokinesis results in
options: a multinucleate condition called syncytium, as in the liquid endosperm of coconut
explanation: Free nuclear division produces many nuclei in a common cytoplasm.

text: If the DNA content of a diploid cell at G₁ is 2C, its DNA content at G₂ and after meiosis II will be, respectively,
explanation: DNA doubles in S phase (2C → 4C); meiosis I halves it to 2C and meiosis II to 1C.

text: An onion root tip cell has 16 chromosomes. How many chromosomes will a cell of the root tip have at anaphase (counting separated chromatids as chromosomes)?
explanation: At anaphase centromeres split and each chromatid becomes a daughter chromosome, so 2 × 16 = 32 move to the poles.

text: Which feature distinguishes prophase I of meiosis from prophase of mitosis?
options: Pairing of homologous chromosomes and crossing over
explanation: Condensation, nucleolus disappearance and nuclear envelope breakdown occur in both; synapsis and crossing over are unique to meiosis I.

text: The correct sequence of substages of prophase I is
explanation: Mnemonic: 'Lazy Zebras Prefer Dull Days'.

text: The movement of water molecules across a selectively permeable membrane from a region of higher water potential to lower water potential is
explanation: Osmosis is a special type of diffusion of water across a differentially permeable membrane.

text: Water potential of pure water at standard temperature and atmospheric pressure is
explanation: Pure water has the greatest water potential, defined as zero; adding solutes lowers it to negative values.

text: Swelling of dry seeds and wooden doors in the rainy season is due to
explanation: Imbibition is absorption of water by hydrophilic colloids such as cellulose and proteins, causing swelling.

text: Loss of water in the form of liquid droplets from the leaf margins through hydathodes is
explanation: Guttation occurs at night or early morning when root pressure is high and transpiration is low, as in grasses.

text: Most transpiration takes place through
explanation: Stomata account for most water loss; small amounts are lost through cuticle and lenticels.

text: Food in plants (mainly sucrose) is translocated through the
explanation: Phloem carries organic solutes from source to sink; xylem carries water and minerals upward.

text: When a plant cell is placed in a hypertonic solution, the protoplast shrinks away from the cell wall. This is called
explanation: Water moves out (exosmosis) to the solution of lower water potential; the reverse on placing it in a hypotonic solution is deplasmolysis.

text: Water potential (Ψw) of a cell is given by
explanation: Solute potential (negative) plus pressure potential (usually positive in turgid cells).

text: Facilitated diffusion differs from simple diffusion in that it
options: requires membrane proteins but no ATP and shows saturation
moves substances against the concentration gradient
explanation: Carriers or channels speed movement down the gradient; transport saturates when all carriers are in use.

text: The pathway of water movement through the cell walls and intercellular spaces, without crossing any membrane, is the
explanation: The apoplast is non-living and continuous through cell walls; the Casparian strip blocks it at the endodermis.

text: The most widely accepted explanation for the ascent of sap in tall trees is
explanation: Transpiration creates tension in xylem; cohesion and adhesion of water maintain a continuous water column.

text: Opening of stomata is accompanied by
options: loss of turgor by guard cells
conversion of sugars into starch in guard cells
efflux of K⁺ ions from guard cells
influx of K⁺ ions into guard cells, lowering their water potential so water enters and they become turgid
explanation: Turgid guard cells bow outward because of radially oriented cellulose microfibrils and thicker inner walls, opening the pore.

text: Symport is a type of transport in which
options: two molecules cross in opposite directions
two molecules cross the membrane in the same direction at the same time
explanation: In antiport they move in opposite directions; in uniport a molecule moves independently.

text: According to the pressure flow (mass flow) hypothesis, sugar is loaded into phloem at the source by
options: active transport, lowering the water potential of the sieve tube so that water enters by osmosis and builds pressure
explanation: Pressure drives the phloem sap to the sink, where sugar is unloaded and water leaves.

text: Root pressure can be demonstrated by
options: exudation of sap from the cut stump of a plant cut near the soil level in the morning
explanation: Ions actively transported into the xylem raise its osmotic pressure, pushing water up a short distance.

text: Which of the following is an advantage of transpiration to a plant?
options: It creates transpiration pull, supplies water for photosynthesis, helps carry minerals and cools leaf surfaces
It increases the weight of the plant
explanation: Transpiration has several benefits though it also causes water loss; it is called a necessary evil.

text: A cell with Ψs = −0.8 MPa and Ψp = 0.3 MPa is placed in a solution of Ψ = −0.6 MPa. What will happen?
options: Water will leave the cell, since the cell's Ψw (−0.5 MPa) is higher than that of the solution
There will be no net movement of water
explanation: Ψw = −0.8 + 0.3 = −0.5 MPa; water moves from higher (−0.5) to lower (−0.6) water potential, i.e. out of the cell.

text: Which statement about C₄ plants and transpiration is correct?
options: C₄ plants keep stomata open throughout the night only
C₄ plants can fix CO₂ efficiently at lower internal CO₂ concentration and so lose about half as much water as C₃ plants for the same amount of CO₂ fixed
C₄ plants lose twice as much water as C₃ plants
explanation: Greater CO₂-fixing efficiency lets C₄ plants partially close stomata and conserve water.

text: Which of the following best explains why the Casparian strip forces water to enter the symplast at the endodermis?
options: The cortex is made of lignified cells
The suberised band in the radial and tangential walls of endodermal cells is impermeable to water
explanation: Water must pass through the plasma membrane of endodermal cells, allowing the plant to regulate solute uptake.

text: Two adjacent cells A and B have water potentials of −0.4 MPa and −0.7 MPa respectively. Which statement is correct?
options: Water moves from A to B
Water moves from B to A
Water moves in both directions equally
explanation: Water moves from higher (less negative) to lower (more negative) water potential: −0.4 is higher than −0.7.

text: The technique of growing plants in a nutrient solution without soil is
explanation: Julius von Sachs (1860) first demonstrated soil-less growth of plants.

text: Which of the following is a micronutrient?
explanation: Micronutrients are needed in very small amounts (less than 10 mmole/kg dry matter): Fe, Mn, Cu, Mo, Zn, B, Cl, Ni.

text: The central atom of the chlorophyll molecule is
explanation: Mg²⁺ is part of the porphyrin ring of chlorophyll.

text: The enzyme responsible for biological nitrogen fixation is
explanation: Nitrogenase, present only in prokaryotes, reduces N₂ to NH₃.

text: Rhizobium forms root nodules in
options: leguminous plants such as pea and gram
explanation: Rhizobium is symbiotic with legumes; Frankia forms nodules on non-leguminous Alnus.

text: Chlorosis, the loss of chlorophyll leading to yellowing of leaves, is caused by deficiency of
options: N, K, Mg, S, Fe, Mn, Zn or Mo
explanation: Chlorosis is a common symptom of deficiency of several elements involved in chlorophyll formation or function.

text: The red-pink colour of active root nodules is due to
explanation: Leghaemoglobin acts as an oxygen scavenger, protecting nitrogenase from oxygen.

text: Nitrification, the oxidation of ammonia to nitrite and then nitrate, is carried out by
explanation: Ammonia → nitrite by Nitrosomonas or Nitrococcus; nitrite → nitrate by Nitrobacter. Pseudomonas and Thiobacillus cause denitrification.

text: Which element is an activator of nitrogenase and is needed for nitrogen fixation?
explanation: Molybdenum is a component of nitrogenase and nitrate reductase.

text: Deficiency symptoms of mobile elements such as N, K and Mg appear first in
explanation: Mobile elements are mobilised from senescing older tissue to younger leaves, so older leaves show symptoms first.

text: Calcium deficiency symptoms appear first in young tissues because calcium
options: is relatively immobile, being a structural component of the cell (middle lamella)
explanation: Elements like Ca and S that are structural components are not easily remobilised.

text: The element required for the splitting of water during photosynthesis, with chlorine, is
explanation: Mn and Cl are involved in the water-splitting (oxygen-evolving) complex associated with PS II.

text: The process by which ammonium ion combines with α-ketoglutaric acid to form glutamic acid is
explanation: Transamination transfers an amino group from one amino acid to a keto acid; glutamic acid is the main donor.

text: Which of the following is a free-living aerobic nitrogen-fixing bacterium?
explanation: Azotobacter and Beijerinckia are free-living aerobes; Rhodospirillum is anaerobic; Rhizobium and Frankia are symbiotic.

text: The initial rapid uptake of ions into the free space (apoplast) of root cells is
options: always against the concentration gradient in free space
passive, while the slower uptake into the inner space (symplast) is active and requires metabolic energy
explanation: Mineral ions move passively into the outer space, then are actively absorbed into cells.

text: Toxicity of manganese can induce deficiency of
explanation: Mn competes with Fe and Mg for uptake and with Mg for binding to enzymes, and inhibits Ca translocation to the shoot apex; brown spots surrounded by chlorotic veins are a symptom.

text: Nitrogenase is highly sensitive to oxygen. In a root nodule it is protected mainly by
explanation: Leghaemoglobin keeps free O₂ low while still supplying the bacteroids for respiration.

text: The overall reaction catalysed by nitrogenase requires approximately how many ATP to fix one molecule of N₂?
options: 16 ATP (with 8 e⁻ and 8 H⁺, producing 2NH₃ and H₂)
explanation: N₂ + 8e⁻ + 8H⁺ + 16ATP → 2NH₃ + H₂ + 16ADP + 16Pi. The energy comes from the host plant's respiration.

text: Which statement about the criteria of essentiality of an element (Arnon and Stout) is correct?
options: The element must be present in large amounts
Any element found in plant ash is essential
The element must be directly involved in metabolism and its requirement must be specific, not replaceable by another element
The element need only increase growth
explanation: An essential element is absolutely needed for normal growth and reproduction, is specific and is directly involved in metabolism.

text: At physiological pH, the amide asparagine is formed from aspartic acid. Amides like asparagine and glutamine are important because they
options: contain more nitrogen than amino acids and are transported to other parts of the plant via xylem
explanation: Amides are formed by replacing the hydroxyl part of an amino acid with another NH₂; in soybean, ureides are transported in xylem.

text: The chief pigment responsible for trapping light in photosynthesis, which forms the reaction centre, is
explanation: Chlorophyll a (bright or blue-green in chromatography) is the main pigment; others are accessory pigments.

text: The light reactions of photosynthesis take place in the
explanation: Light reactions occur on thylakoid membranes; the Calvin cycle occurs in the stroma.

text: The oxygen released during photosynthesis comes from
explanation: Ruben and Kamen used ¹⁸O to show that O₂ evolved comes from H₂O (also deduced by van Niel).

text: The first stable product of CO₂ fixation in C₃ plants is
explanation: RuBisCO fixes CO₂ with RuBP to give two molecules of 3-PGA, a three-carbon compound.

text: The primary CO₂ acceptor in the C₄ pathway is
explanation: PEP carboxylase in mesophyll cells fixes CO₂ into oxaloacetic acid, a four-carbon compound.

text: The reaction centre of photosystem I has an absorption peak at
explanation: PS I reaction centre is P700; PS II reaction centre is P680.

text: In cyclic photophosphorylation
options: water is split to release oxygen
both PS I and PS II are involved and NADPH is formed
only PS I is involved; ATP is produced but not NADPH, and no O₂ is evolved
explanation: Electrons return from the acceptor to PS I through the electron transport chain; it occurs in stroma lamellae, which lack PS II and NADP reductase.

text: The splitting of water during the light reaction is associated with
explanation: The water-splitting complex is on the inner (lumen) side of the thylakoid membrane and supplies electrons to PS II.

text: According to the chemiosmotic hypothesis, ATP is synthesised in chloroplasts because
options: CO₂ breaks down into carbon and oxygen
electrons are absorbed by ATP synthase
a proton gradient across the thylakoid membrane drives protons through ATP synthase (CF₀–CF₁)
light directly combines ADP and phosphate
explanation: Protons accumulate in the lumen from water splitting and plastoquinone; their flow back to the stroma through CF₀ provides energy for CF₁ to make ATP.

text: For the synthesis of one molecule of glucose through the Calvin cycle, the requirement is
explanation: Each CO₂ fixed requires 3 ATP and 2 NADPH; six turns of the cycle (6 CO₂) need 18 ATP and 12 NADPH.

text: Kranz anatomy, with large bundle sheath cells arranged in a wreath around vascular bundles, is characteristic of
options: C₄ plants such as maize and sugarcane
C₃ plants such as wheat and rice
explanation: Bundle sheath cells of C₄ plants have many chloroplasts, thick walls impervious to gases and no intercellular spaces.

text: In C₄ plants, the Calvin cycle takes place in
explanation: Malate/aspartate formed in mesophyll moves to bundle sheath cells, where it is decarboxylated and CO₂ enters the Calvin cycle with RuBisCO.

text: Photorespiration differs from normal photosynthesis in that
options: it produces extra ATP and NADPH
it occurs only in C₄ plants
RuBisCO binds O₂ instead of CO₂, forming one molecule of PGA and phosphoglycolate, with no ATP or sugar gain
explanation: Photorespiration is a wasteful process occurring in C₃ plants; C₄ plants avoid it by concentrating CO₂ around RuBisCO.

text: Blackman's law of limiting factors states that when a process is conditioned by several factors, its rate is limited by
options: all factors equally at the same time
the factor present at the lowest (minimum) value relative to its requirement
the factor present in the highest amount
explanation: Changing the limiting factor alone changes the rate; increasing other factors has no effect.

text: Which pair of organelles cooperates with the chloroplast in photorespiration?
explanation: Glycolate from the chloroplast is metabolised in peroxisomes and mitochondria, where CO₂ is released.

text: The action spectrum of photosynthesis shows maximum activity in
options: blue and red regions of the spectrum
explanation: The action spectrum closely follows the absorption spectrum of chlorophyll a, with peaks in blue and red light.

text: Six turns of the Calvin cycle fix how many molecules of CO₂ and regenerate how many RuBP?
explanation: Each turn fixes one CO₂ on one RuBP; six turns fix 6 CO₂ (one hexose) and regenerate the 6 RuBP used.

text: Why do C₄ plants show higher productivity than C₃ plants in hot, dry, high-light conditions?
options: C₄ plants do not need light
PEP carboxylase concentrates CO₂ in bundle sheath cells, suppressing RuBisCO's oxygenase activity and photorespiration
explanation: High CO₂ around RuBisCO prevents photorespiration; C₄ plants also tolerate higher temperatures and have a higher temperature optimum.

text: Engelmann's experiment with Cladophora and aerobic bacteria showed that
options: no oxygen was released in any light
bacteria collected only in the green region
aerobic bacteria accumulated in the blue and red regions of the split spectrum, indicating oxygen evolution there
explanation: He used a prism to split light and obtained the first action spectrum of photosynthesis.

text: In the Z-scheme of non-cyclic photophosphorylation, the correct path of electrons is
options: H₂O → PS I → PS II → NADP⁺
NADP⁺ → PS I → PS II → H₂O
H₂O → PS II → electron transport chain (incl. cytochromes) → PS I → NADP⁺
PS I → H₂O → PS II → NADP⁺
explanation: Electrons from water fill PS II; excited electrons pass downhill through the ETC to PS I and are finally used to reduce NADP⁺ to NADPH + H⁺.

text: Glycolysis takes place in the
explanation: Glycolysis (EMP pathway) occurs in the cytoplasm of all living organisms.

text: The end product of glycolysis is
explanation: One glucose gives two molecules of pyruvic acid.

text: In yeast, anaerobic respiration (alcoholic fermentation) produces
explanation: Pyruvate → acetaldehyde (pyruvic acid decarboxylase) → ethanol (alcohol dehydrogenase).

text: The Krebs cycle occurs in the
explanation: Krebs (TCA/citric acid) cycle enzymes are in the matrix, except succinate dehydrogenase, which is on the inner membrane.

text: The final acceptor of electrons in the electron transport system is
explanation: O₂ accepts electrons and protons to form water at complex IV.

text: Respiratory quotient (RQ) is the ratio of
options: volume of O₂ consumed to CO₂ evolved
volume of CO₂ evolved to volume of O₂ consumed
explanation: RQ = CO₂ evolved / O₂ consumed.

text: The RQ of carbohydrates during aerobic respiration is
explanation: C₆H₁₂O₆ + 6O₂ → 6CO₂ + 6H₂O; 6CO₂/6O₂ = 1.0. Fats give about 0.7 and proteins about 0.9.

text: Lactic acid fermentation in muscles during vigorous exercise involves reduction of pyruvic acid by
options: NADH + H⁺ catalysed by lactate dehydrogenase
explanation: NADH is reoxidised to NAD⁺, allowing glycolysis to continue under oxygen deficiency.

text: Pyruvic acid is converted to acetyl CoA by oxidative decarboxylation in the
options: mitochondrial matrix, catalysed by pyruvate dehydrogenase
explanation: Pyruvic acid + CoA + NAD⁺ → acetyl CoA + CO₂ + NADH + H⁺, requiring Mg²⁺ and the pyruvate dehydrogenase complex.

text: The first product of the Krebs cycle formed by condensation of acetyl CoA with oxaloacetic acid is
explanation: Citrate synthase catalyses formation of six-carbon citric acid, so it is also called the citric acid cycle.

text: How many molecules of NADH are produced per molecule of acetyl CoA oxidised in the Krebs cycle?
explanation: Each turn yields 3 NADH, 1 FADH₂, 1 GTP/ATP and 2 CO₂.

text: Substrate-level phosphorylation in the Krebs cycle occurs during the conversion of
explanation: This step produces one GTP (converted to ATP).

text: In the electron transport system, complex IV is
options: cytochrome c oxidase, containing cytochromes a and a₃ and copper centres
explanation: Complex I is NADH dehydrogenase, II succinate dehydrogenase, III cytochrome bc₁, IV cytochrome c oxidase, V ATP synthase.

text: The respiratory pathway is called amphibolic because
options: it is involved in both breakdown (catabolism) and synthesis (anabolism) of molecules
it produces both ATP and ADP
it occurs both in mitochondria and chloroplasts
it uses both O₂ and CO₂
explanation: Intermediates are withdrawn for synthesis of fatty acids, amino acids and other molecules.

text: Electrons from FADH₂ enter the electron transport system at
explanation: FADH₂ bypasses complex I, so it yields fewer ATP (2) than NADH (3).

text: Fatty acids enter the respiratory pathway after being broken down to
explanation: Fats are broken to glycerol (converted to PGAL) and fatty acids (degraded to acetyl CoA).

text: Assuming each NADH yields 3 ATP and each FADH₂ yields 2 ATP, the net gain of ATP from aerobic respiration of one glucose molecule is
explanation: Glycolysis: 2 ATP + 2 NADH (6 ATP); link reaction: 2 NADH (6); Krebs: 2 ATP + 6 NADH (18) + 2 FADH₂ (4). Total = 2 + 6 + 6 + 2 + 18 + 4 = 38.

text: Calculate the RQ of tripalmitin given: 2C₅₁H₉₈O₆ + 145O₂ → 102CO₂ + 98H₂O + energy.
How many ATP are produced net per glucose in alcoholic fermentation?
explanation: Glycolysis produces 4 ATP and uses 2, net 2; fermentation steps produce no ATP, and NADH is used to make ethanol.

text: Which statement about ATP synthase (complex V) is correct?
options: It pumps protons into the matrix using ATP
It is located in the outer mitochondrial membrane
F₀ is the membrane-embedded proton channel and F₁ is the headpiece where ATP is synthesised from ADP and Pi
F₁ forms the proton channel and F₀ synthesises ATP
explanation: Protons flow from the intermembrane space to the matrix through F₀, and the energy drives ATP synthesis at F₁.

text: Malic acid, an organic acid, is respired according to C₄H₆O₅ + 3O₂ → 4CO₂ + 3H₂O. Its RQ is
explanation: RQ = 4/3 = 1.33. Organic acids have RQ greater than one because they are rich in oxygen.

text: The plant hormone that promotes cell division and delays leaf senescence is
explanation: Cytokinins promote cytokinesis, new leaf and chloroplast formation, and the Richmond–Lang effect (delay of senescence).

text: Which plant growth regulator is a gas?
explanation: Ethylene is a simple gaseous PGR that promotes fruit ripening and senescence.

text: Abscisic acid is often called the
explanation: ABA increases tolerance to stresses, induces stomatal closure and promotes seed dormancy.

text: The hormone used to promote ripening of fruits such as bananas and tomatoes is
explanation: Ethephon, which releases ethylene, hastens fruit ripening.

text: The response of plants to the relative length of day and night is
explanation: Garner and Allard first described photoperiodism in tobacco.

text: Promotion of flowering by exposure to low temperature is
explanation: Biennials and winter varieties of wheat and barley need cold treatment to flower.

text: The phenomenon in which the apical bud suppresses the growth of lateral buds is
options: apical dominance, controlled mainly by auxin
explanation: Removal of the shoot tip (decapitation) results in growth of lateral buds; used in tea plantations and hedge-making.

text: Bolting, the sudden elongation of internodes just prior to flowering in rosette plants such as cabbage, is promoted by
explanation: Gibberellins promote internode elongation in rosette plants.

text: 2,4-D is widely used to
options: kill broad-leaved dicot weeds without affecting mature monocot plants
explanation: 2,4-D is a synthetic auxin used as a selective weedicide.

text: The phase of growth in which cells increase in size and vacuolation, with new cell wall deposition, is the
explanation: Growth phases: meristematic (division), elongation (enlargement), maturation (differentiation).

text: Growth in which the rate of growth is constant, and plotting length against time gives a straight line, is
explanation: In arithmetic growth only one daughter cell keeps dividing: Lₜ = L₀ + rt.

text: Differentiated cells that regain the capacity to divide, as in the formation of interfascicular cambium and cork cambium, undergo
explanation: Cells derived from dedifferentiated tissue later mature and lose the capacity to divide again (redifferentiation).

text: Gibberellins are used commercially to
options: increase the length of grape stalks and increase sugarcane yield by lengthening the stem
explanation: Spraying sugarcane with GAs increases stem length and yield by up to 20 tonnes per acre; GAs also hasten malting in brewing.

text: The site of perception of the photoperiodic stimulus in plants is the
explanation: Leaves perceive the light/dark period, and a hormonal 'florigen' is thought to move to shoot apices.

text: Cytokinins were first discovered as 'kinetin' from
explanation: Skoog and Miller isolated kinetin (a modified adenine) from herring sperm DNA; zeatin was later found in corn kernels and coconut milk.

text: Which of the following effects is caused by ethylene?
options: Promoting horizontal growth of seedlings, swelling of the axis and apical hook formation in dicot seedlings
explanation: This 'triple response' is characteristic of ethylene; it also promotes senescence and abscission.

text: A leaf grows from 4 cm² to 9 cm² in one week. Its absolute growth and relative growth rate over the week are
explanation: Absolute growth = 9 − 4 = 5 cm². Relative growth = 5/4 × 100 = 125%.

text: A short-day plant flowers when exposed to
options: a day length longer than a critical period
a dark period longer than a critical length
explanation: It is the duration of the uninterrupted dark period that is critical for short-day plants; interrupting it with a flash of light prevents flowering.

text: Which statement about abscisic acid (ABA) is correct?
options: It promotes cell division in tissue culture
It acts as a general growth inhibitor, inhibits seed germination, and is antagonistic to gibberellins
explanation: ABA induces dormancy and stomatal closure; GAs break dormancy and promote germination.

text: In geometric growth, if one cell divides mitotically and both daughter cells continue to divide, after 5 generations the number of cells will be
explanation: Geometric growth gives 2ⁿ cells: 2⁵ = 32. This is described by W₁ = W₀eʳᵗ.

text: Plasticity in plants is shown by heterophylly. Which is an example of heterophylly caused by the environment?
options: Larkspur, with different leaves in juvenile and adult stages
Coriander, whose basal and upper leaves differ
Buttercup, whose submerged leaves differ in shape from leaves above water
Cotton, whose juvenile leaves differ from mature leaves
explanation: Leaf-shape differences in cotton, coriander and larkspur are due to developmental stage; in buttercup they are environmentally induced.

text: The dental formula of an adult human (half of upper jaw / half of lower jaw) is
explanation: Incisors 2, canine 1, premolars 2, molars 3 in each half jaw: 32 teeth in all.

text: The largest gland of the human body is the
explanation: The liver weighs about 1.2–1.5 kg in an adult.

text: Salivary amylase acts on
options: fats, converting them to fatty acids
explanation: About 30% of starch is hydrolysed in the mouth by salivary amylase at pH 6.8.

text: The finger-like projections of the small intestinal mucosa that increase the absorptive surface are
explanation: Villi with microvilli give a brush-border appearance and enormously increase surface area.

text: Bile is stored in the
explanation: Bile, secreted by hepatic cells, is concentrated and stored in the gall bladder.

text: Hydrochloric acid in the stomach is secreted by the
explanation: Chief cells secrete pepsinogen; goblet cells secrete mucus.

text: Pepsinogen is converted to the active enzyme pepsin by
explanation: HCl provides an acidic pH (about 1.8) and activates pepsinogen; enterokinase activates trypsinogen in the intestine.

text: Trypsinogen is activated to trypsin by
options: enterokinase secreted by the intestinal mucosa
explanation: Trypsin then activates other pancreatic zymogens such as chymotrypsinogen and procarboxypeptidases.

text: Bile helps in digestion of fats by
options: emulsifying fats into small micelles, and it activates lipase
explanation: Bile contains no digestive enzymes; bile salts emulsify fats, increasing the surface area for lipase.

text: Fatty acids and glycerol, being insoluble, are absorbed by being incorporated into micelles, then re-formed into
options: chylomicrons that are transported into the lacteals (lymph vessels) of villi
explanation: Chylomicrons are small protein-coated fat globules released into lacteals and finally into the blood.

text: Rennin, found in the gastric juice of infants, helps in
options: digestion of milk proteins by curdling
explanation: Rennin converts casein to paracasein in the presence of Ca²⁺.

text: The hormone that stimulates the pancreas to release bicarbonate-rich pancreatic juice is
explanation: Secretin from duodenal cells acts on pancreatic ducts; CCK stimulates enzyme secretion and gall bladder contraction.

text: Which of the following substances is absorbed by active transport in the small intestine?
explanation: Glucose and amino acids are absorbed by carrier-mediated active transport against concentration gradients; water moves by osmosis.

text: The opening of the stomach into the duodenum is guarded by the
explanation: The gastro-oesophageal (cardiac) sphincter is at the oesophagus–stomach junction; the sphincter of Oddi guards the common hepato-pancreatic duct.

text: Which disorder is caused by inflammation of the liver, often due to viral infection, and results in yellowing of skin and eyes?
explanation: In jaundice the liver is affected and bile pigments are deposited in the skin and eyes.

text: Kupffer cells in the liver are
options: cells that store vitamin A only
explanation: Kupffer cells are macrophages that remove bacteria and worn-out cells from blood in the liver.

text: Which enzyme acts on the products of protein digestion (dipeptides) in the intestinal juice (succus entericus)?
explanation: Dipeptidases convert dipeptides to amino acids; maltase, lactase and sucrase act on disaccharides; nucleotidases and nucleosidases act on nucleic acid products.

text: Which intestinal enzyme is correctly matched with its action?
explanation: Lactase acts on lactose; maltase on maltose; nucleases on nucleic acids.

text: The Brunner's glands are found in the
